client: I've been really struggling with work lately. My boss just dumped two huge new projects on me with impossible deadlines, and I'm already drowning in my current workload. I don't even know if talking about this will help - the work isn't going away no matter what we discuss here.
therapist:
I hear both frustration and urgency in your voice as you describe this overwhelming situation at work. The way you're describing these demands makes me wonder if you're feeling trapped—like no matter what you do, it won't be enough. 

Could we look at what thoughts might be making this situation feel particularly impossible right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, it does feel impossible sometimes. The main thought running through my head is "I'm going to fail no matter what I do." Even when I complete tasks, there's always more piling up, and I can't shake the feeling that I'm barely keeping my head above water. 

I know rationally that not everything is life-or-death, but it *feels* that way in the moment. Like if I make one wrong move, everything will collapse.
therapist: Your voice sounds quietly strained as you describe this exhausting cycle—it seems like you're carrying not just the workload, but also this heavy certainty of failure. That gap between knowing "rationally" and *feeling* the weight of collapse is exactly where we can work—would you be willing to explore what evidence might challenge this "wrong move" catastrophe prediction?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I know logically that one mistake at work won't ruin everything, but I can't shake this dread that if I slip up even once, the whole house of cards will collapse. It feels like everyone else can make small errors without consequences, but for me it would be catastrophic. I'm not sure what evidence would help because my anxiety tells me "this time is different."
therapist:
I hear how real and paralyzing this fear feels—your voice tightens when you describe that "house of cards" scenario, like you're bracing for impact. That "this time is different" thought is particularly powerful because it overrides even what you know to be logically true.

Would it help to examine together what this anxiety might be protecting you from? Sometimes catastrophizing functions like an overzealous guard trying to prevent any possible disappointment.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: But what if the anxiety isn't protecting me from anything? What if it's just my brain malfunctioning? I've tried telling myself it's irrational before, but that never stops the physical feeling - the tight chest, the shaky hands. It just makes me feel more broken.
therapist:
Your voice speeds up as you describe this—it sounds like you're not just frustrated with the anxiety, but also with the ways you've tried to fight it that haven't worked. That sense of being "broken" adds another painful layer when you're already feeling overwhelmed.  

Instead of focusing on whether the anxiety is rational, could we look at how responding to these physical sensations with curiosity rather than judgment might shift things? The tight chest and shaky hands are signals—what if we tried understanding them instead of silencing them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about curiosity instead of judgment, but it’s hard to even imagine doing that. When my chest tightens or my hands shake, all I can think is, "This shouldn’t be happening," and I spiral into panic. It feels like my body is betraying me, and trying to be curious about it just seems... impossible. How am I supposed to shift my mindset when I’m already drowning in fear?
therapist:
Your voice has a fragile quality as you describe this—like you're holding both exhaustion and resignation about these overwhelming physical reactions. That gap between knowing curiosity could help and feeling unable to access it must feel incredibly frustrating.  

Would it feel more manageable if we started smaller—maybe just noticing one breath at a time rather than trying to shift the entire mindset at once? Even naming "this is fear" without judgment can create a tiny bit of space.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, slow speech

client:
I appreciate you noticing how exhausted I feel about this. But honestly, even focusing on one breath feels impossible right now—my mind just races ahead to all the "what if" scenarios. When you suggest naming the fear, it makes me feel more anxious because then I start analyzing why I'm afraid, which just makes it worse. 

I know you're trying to help, but these small steps still feel like too much when my body is already in panic mode. It's like telling someone drowning to just focus on one drop of water at a time.
therapist:
Your voice sounds both weary and rushed—like you're caught between exhaustion and that relentless mental churn of "what ifs." I hear how even well-meaning suggestions feel impossible when panic has such a strong grip, almost like your mind and body are working against you right now.  

Instead of trying to change anything in this moment, would it help to simply acknowledge together how utterly overwhelming this feels? Sometimes naming that overwhelm—without any expectation to fix it—can take some of its power away.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, it does feel overwhelming. Like my brain won’t stop running through worst-case scenarios, and even when I know it’s irrational, I can’t shake the dread. But I don’t know if just naming it helps—it feels like I’m stuck in this loop no matter what I do.  

Sometimes it’s worse when people tell me to just "acknowledge" the anxiety, because then I feel like I’m admitting defeat to it. Like if I say it out loud, it becomes more real.
therapist:
Your voice sounds both weary and tense—like you're carrying this heavy dread while also bracing against it. That fear of "admitting defeat" makes so much sense when anxiety has felt like an enemy you have to outthink or outrun.  

What if we reframed this not as surrender, but as noticing the storm without being swept away by it? The fact that you're here, putting words to this struggle, already shows how much strength you have even when it doesn't feel that way.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I like the idea of not seeing my anxiety as an enemy to fight, but it's hard to imagine just "noticing" it without reacting. Whenever I try that, the physical symptoms hit me so hard—racing heart, tight chest—that I panic and feel like I'm losing control. 

Part of me wants to believe I can handle it differently, but another part thinks "noticing the storm" sounds too passive when the storm feels like it's destroying me. How do you actually do that without just feeling helpless?
therapist:
I hear both the conflict and the physical distress in your voice—it speeds up when you describe the racing heart and tightness, like your body is sounding an alarm. That tension between wanting to believe change is possible and fearing helplessness makes complete sense when panic feels so visceral.  

What if we thought of "noticing" not as passivity, but as the first step in choosing how to respond? Like seeing dark clouds and deciding whether to brace for rain or reach for an umbrella—the storm isn't yours to control, but your relationship to it can shift.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I like the idea of noticing as an active choice, but when I’m in the middle of a panic attack, it feels impossible to think that way. My mind just spirals, and I can’t separate myself from it—it’s like I *am* the storm. I worry that trying to notice it in the moment will just make me feel more overwhelmed.
therapist:
Your voice softens and quickens as you describe this—it sounds like panic wraps around you so tightly that it becomes hard to see where *you* end and the storm begins. That fear of feeling more overwhelmed when trying to notice makes complete sense when you're already caught in that spiral.  

Would it help to practice noticing in calmer moments first, like building a life raft before you're in the waves? That way, when panic hits, you might feel more anchored to something familiar.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about building a life raft, but I’m not sure it’ll help when I’m in the middle of a panic attack. Those moments feel so different from when I’m calm—it’s like I forget everything I’ve practiced. Plus, I don’t even know where to start with noticing in calmer moments. It feels like I’m just waiting for the next wave to hit.
therapist:
Your voice sounds quieter and higher-pitched as you share this—like you're caught between resignation and a lingering hope for something to change. That gap between calm moments and panic attacks can feel so vast, making it hard to trust that any preparation will help when the waves hit.  

What if we started with something small, like noticing just one sensation when you're feeling steady—maybe the texture of your shirt or the weight of your feet on the floor? It’s not about stopping the waves, but building a tiny anchor you can hold onto when they come.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
